title: From Mitochondrial Support to Mitohormetic Readiness: Micronutrient Determinants of the Energy Allocation System
content: This review proposes that selected micronutrients may contribute to mitohormetic readiness, defined as the biochemical and regulatory capacity to sense, buffer, transduce, and recover from adaptive mitochondrial stress in a manner that promotes resilience rather than maladaptation. This nutrient-centered construct extends the Energy Allocation System (EAS) framework, in which resilience is constrained by how organisms allocate finite metabolic resources under stress, with conservation-dominant phenotypes reflecting coordinated energy-conserving responses rather than isolated dysfunction. This review argues that micronutrients may matter less because they directly stimulate mitochondria and more because they help preserve the endocrine, redox, enzymatic, and one-carbon conditions required for beneficial adaptation. Thyroid physiology is used as the clearest exemplar of nutrient-enabled adaptive pacing, particularly through the roles of iodine, selenium, and iron, and the interpretive orientation is then broadened to include methylfolate, cobalamin, riboflavin, magnesium, and niacin. The goal is not to present a finalized mechanistic proof, but to offer a hypothesis-generating extension of EAS that may refine how resilience, metabolic flexibility, and biochemical sufficiency are interpreted in clinical bioenergetics.
